children: Oil prices fell Friday after surging in the previous session, as traders assessed growing risks to Middle East crude exports following fresh territorial gains by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.

Front-month Brent crude oil futures fell 3.8% to $103.51 a barrel, while front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures dropped 3.5% to $98.85 a barrel. Both benchmarks settled Thursday at their highest closing levels since May 19, with Brent at $107.63 and WTI at $102.48.

Shipping around the Strait of Hormuz remained under pressure, with the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations saying Thursday that four unidentified projectiles struck two vessels near Khasab, Oman, causing a fire on one.

Meanwhile, Houthi militants captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim island. Perim sits inside the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and divides the narrow waterway into two shipping channels, putting the group in a stronger position to threaten vessels entering or leaving the Red Sea.

The move raises fresh risks around the Red Sea at a time when Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the route to circumvent disruptions in the Persian Gulf. The kingdom's crude production fell by roughly 1.9 million barrels a day to 6.24 million barrels a day in August, down 23% from July, according to the latest data from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
ANZ Research analysts said the advance could give the Houthis a foothold that would enable the group to almost fully control the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

The pullback in crude follows a sharp rally Thursday, when WTI surged 6.7% and Brent gained 6.3% as intensifying fighting across the region fueled concerns over global energy supplies. Oil futures had moved into overbought territory and could be due for a corrective phase, Dennis Kissler of BOK Financial said in a note.

The International Energy Agency said a recovery in Middle East oil flows is now expected to stretch into next year as escalating attacks on Gulf shipping and Houthi threats in the Red Sea keep key energy arteries under strain. The energy watchdog--a group of Western nations and their allies--further cut its outlook for global oil demand, now expecting consumption to fall by 2.5 million barrels a day in 2026 to 102.4 million barrels a day, compared with its previous forecast for a 1.6-million-barrel-a-day decline.
